title: 'Go Home' Row Escalates: Krishnamoorthi Doubles Down as Dhillon Reveals Daily Racist Attacks
excerpt: What began as a Florida councilman's 'take your curry and go home' jibe has widened into a bipartisan reckoning, with Trump's civil rights chief disclosing identity attacks and new data showing half of Indian Americans report discrimination.
body:
• The "take your curry and go home" dispute has widened into a national argument about belonging: Harmeet Dhillon, the Trump administration's assistant attorney general for civil rights, says she faces racist comments daily, including being called a "paperwork American."
  • A 2026 Carnegie Endowment survey found that one in two Indian Americans reported experiencing discrimination in the previous year.
  • Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi's rebuke — "I'm staying. So is the curry. America is my home." — has become the emblematic answer to Palm Bay councilman Chandler Langevin's jibe.
  • The attacks cross party lines: Nikki Haley, Vivek Ramaswamy and Usha Vance have also faced identity-based attacks, according to India Weekly's reporting.

What began as a Florida city councilman's "take your curry and go home" jibe at a sitting US congressman has widened into a national argument about who counts as American — with a senior Trump administration official now saying she faces the same identity attacks from the opposite end of the political spectrum.

The latest flashpoint

The exchange started on September 11, when Palm Bay City Councilman Chandler Langevin wrote on X: "I won Rajesh. Take your curry and go home," directing the remark at US Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, an Illinois Democrat and one of the most prominent Indian-origin lawmakers in Congress.

"I'm staying. So is the curry. America is my home. No bigot gets to decide who is American, who belongs here, or what they have for dinner. That's the America I'll always fight for."

— Raja Krishnamoorthi, US Representative (D-Illinois)

The trigger came a day earlier, when Krishnamoorthi condemned a Department of Homeland Security social media post styled as a movie poster featuring a man identified as "Mr. Singh." The post told the man to "get off our roads" and warned him to "self-deport or find out." Langevin has used "Rajesh" — a reference to a character on the sitcom The Big Bang Theory — as an epithet for the congressman since October 2025.

A pattern, not an incident

The remark was not isolated. Langevin has been under scrutiny since 2025 for a string of social media posts targeting Indian immigrants, including calls to "deport every Indian immediately" and posts describing Krishnamoorthi as a "foreign occupier" with his country of origin listed as "Tatooine," the fictional planet from Star Wars.

Florida Today reported on September 15 that Langevin had continued the attacks this month, including a post calling Indians "foreigners invading our country." The Palm Bay City Council voted 4-1 in October 2025 to ask Governor Ron DeSantis to suspend Langevin from office, and later voted 3-2 to censure him. Langevin sued the city alleging a First Amendment violation; the case settled in February 2026 for $55,000.

Across the aisle

What gives the row its new weight is that the same question of belonging is now being raised by figures on the political right. Harmeet K. Dhillon, the Trump administration's assistant attorney general for civil rights — born in Chandigarh — recently said she faces racist comments daily, including being called a "paperwork American," which questions the authenticity of her American identity because of her Indian heritage.

Dhillon is not an opponent of the Trump movement. She is part of the administration — yet her experience shows that political alignment does not necessarily prevent ancestry from becoming a target. Former South Carolina governor Nikki Haley has been told to "go back to your own country," Vivek Ramaswamy has faced attacks questioning his American identity, and Usha Vance, the vice president's wife, has been targeted over her Indian ancestry.

As India Weekly put it: if reaching Congress, serving in the administration, running for president or serving as governor is not enough to silence questions about belonging, what exactly is being demanded of Indian Americans to prove that they are American?

The numbers behind the story

The episodes are not only about politicians. The 2026 Indian American Attitudes Survey by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace found that one in two Indian Americans reported experiencing discrimination in the previous year. The nationally representative survey covered 1,000 Indian American adults via YouGov between November 25, 2025, and January 6, 2026.

Indian Americans now number more than 5.2 million, according to Carnegie, and are becoming more politically diverse: Democratic identification fell from 52 percent in 2020 to 46 percent in 2026, while Republican identification rose from 15 percent to 19 percent and independents increased to 29 percent.

What's next

Langevin remains on the Palm Bay council; the 2025 suspension request to DeSantis did not result in his removal. But Krishnamoorthi's reply has turned the attack line itself into the headline. The uncomfortable question it leaves behind: how American do you have to become before someone stops telling you to go back to India?

nri_angle: The episode has become a defining test of belonging for Indian Americans, the community repeatedly targeted in the Florida councilman's remarks.
